393.title: One life, all humanity
393.hook: whoever saves one life, it is as if he saved all humankind (5:32)
393.howItsDone: Muslims often quote 5:32 against murder and terror and in praise of rescuers, doctors and blood donors; scholars teach it together with the story of Adam's two sons in the verses before it and the law in the verse after it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shana'an: hatred that must never bend you from fairness. Your line was just, even then.

Two brothers each bring an offering. One is accepted; one is not. The Qur'an doesn't give their names; Muslim tradition calls them Qabil and Habil, the names many people know as Cain and Abel. The one whose offering was refused says, I will kill you. The other answers with a startling line: even if you stretch out your hand to kill me, I will not stretch out mine to kill you. Then the first brother does it. Afterward he stands over the body with no idea what to do, until a raven lands and scratches at the ground. That's where today's verse comes from.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS, TWO OFFERINGS.` → `I WILL NOT STRETCH OUT MY HAND.` → `A RAVEN SCRATCHING THE GROUND.`

segments.voice: Surah five, verses twenty-seven to thirty-one, tell the brothers. The raven shows the killer how to hide his brother's body, and he cries out, woe is me, am I not even able to be like this raven? He's become, the text says, one of the regretful. Then verse thirty-two draws the lesson: for that cause. In Pickthall's words, whoever kills a human being, except for murder or for spreading corruption in the land, “it shall be as if he had killed all mankind, and whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind.” The word for that one life is nafs: a soul, a self, a person. The Qur'an says this was decreed for the Children of Israel, and the Mishnah, the early collection of Jewish law, teaches something very close: whoever saves one life, scripture counts it as saving a whole world. A neighbor's sentence, kept in two books. Why one for all? Commentators give a few answers. Every person comes from the same first parents, so one death breaks the whole family. A person who kills once has shown he'd kill anyone. And the one who saves a life has defended the very idea that life is sacred. The verse has two halves. People often quote only the first, against killing. The second is just as large, and it's the one you can do on an ordinary day. The next verse, thirty-three, deals with armed robbery and war on the community, and commentators read the two together. The heart of thirty-two stays simple: a single person weighs as much as everyone.

segments.voice: Think of a small life near you, easy to overlook: a spider in the corner, a plant that needs water, a friend who went quiet. Pick one, and picture protecting it in one small act: a cup of water, a knock, a text.
One life. Nafs: one soul. Surah five, verse thirty-two: to save one life is as if to save all humankind. Today's word.
Your line: one life, all life. The second half is the one for ordinary days. That's day three hundred ninety-three.

394.title: Compete in good
394.hook: to each We gave a law and a way; had Allah willed He'd have made one community, so race in good (5:48)
394.howItsDone: Muslims often quote fastabiqu al-khayrat (2:148; 5:48) to encourage charity drives and good works, and 5:48 is often cited when speaking about living alongside people of other faiths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: one life, as if all mankind. Your line was one life, all life. Today, a verse about many communities, and what to do while they differ.

A friendly race can look like this. Two coworkers trying to be first to cover a shift for someone sick. Two sisters each sneaking off to pay the restaurant bill before the other can. Nobody loses, exactly; the point is the thing being raced toward. Surah five has spent several verses on earlier scriptures: the Torah, which it calls guidance and light, then the Gospel given to Isa, then the Qur'an. Then it reaches a verse that asks why there are different communities at all, and gives an answer shaped like a race.
screen: `FIRST TO PAY THE BILL.` → `TORAH, GOSPEL, QUR'AN.` → `WHY MORE THAN ONE COMMUNITY?`

segments.voice: Verse forty-eight, in Pickthall's words: “For each We have appointed a divine law and a traced-out way.” Two Arabic words there. Shir'ah, from the same root as shari'ah, which Arabic lexicons say first named the path down to a watering place, the trail people and animals walk to reach water. And minhaj, a clear, open road. Then: had Allah willed, He could have made you one community. But He didn't, so that He may test you in what He has given you. And then the turn: “So vie one with another in good works.” The Arabic is fastabiqu al-khayrat: race each other toward the good things. The same command appears in surah two. The verse ends by saying everyone returns to Allah, and He will tell them about the things they differed over. Muslim scholars read this in more than one way. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir understood it as each prophet's community receiving its law in its own time, with the Qur'an now the law for Muslims and a guardian over the earlier books. Some Muslim writers today stress the second half: the differences are real, and their settling belongs to God, on the Day, not to us now. Both readings share the practical point. While people differ, the verse doesn't say argue until someone wins. It says race toward the good. Your neighbor's kindness is not a threat to yours. It's the pace you're trying to match.

segments.voice: Somewhere near you is a person who is better at one kind of good: they remember birthdays, or visit the sick, or never gossip. 395.title: Breaking an oath
395.hook: the expiation for a broken oath is feeding ten poor people (5:89)
395.howItsDone: Muslims who break a deliberate oath pay kaffarah, often by feeding ten needy people or giving the equivalent through a mosque or charity; if they can't, they fast three days. Some teachers also discourage swearing by God in everyday talk.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fastabiqu al-khayrat: race each other toward the good. Your line was race in good. Today, what happens when a promise sworn by God goes wrong.

Wallahi. By God. It turns up in plenty of arguments about who ate the last samosa. Wallahi I didn't. Wallahi I'll be there in five minutes. It slips out so easily it barely registers. Then there's the other kind: the oath sworn in earnest, in anger. By God, I will never speak to you again. What does the Qur'an do with someone who swore something like that and now wishes they hadn't? It doesn't shrug. It doesn't trap them either. It hands them a bill, payable to the hungry.
screen: `WALLAHI — BY GOD.` → `NEVER SPEAKING TO YOU AGAIN.` → `A BILL, PAYABLE TO THE HUNGRY.`

segments.voice: Surah five, verse eighty-nine, draws a line between two kinds of oath. The first is laghw, idle talk: oaths that fall out of your mouth without meaning to bind anything. Allah, the verse says, doesn't take you to task for those. A report in Bukhari has Aishah explaining them as the everyday no, by God, and yes, by God, of casual speech. The second kind is sworn deliberately. Break that one, and there's a cost. In Pickthall's words: “The expiation thereof is the feeding of ten of the needy,” with the average of what you feed your own family. Or clothing ten people. Or freeing a slave, an act the Qur'an names as an expiation in other verses too. If none of that is possible, three days of fasting. The word is kaffarah. Arabic dictionaries give its root, k-f-r, the sense of covering over, the way a farmer covers seed with soil. A kaffarah covers a broken word, not by pretending it wasn't broken, but by laying something good on top of it. And there's a twist. A hadith in Bukhari and Muslim says that if someone swears to do something, then sees that something else is better, they should do the better thing and pay the expiation. So in the hadith's logic, an oath never to speak to a brother isn't a cage: the better thing is the phone call, and the expiation is the meal for ten. Near its end, the verse tells believers to guard their oaths. The simplest way to guard them is to swear fewer.

Kaffarah. Expiation: the covering of a broken oath, by feeding ten people, clothing them, freeing someone, or fasting three days. Today's word.
Your line: swear less. A plain yes or no is enough. Day three hundred ninety-five, done.

396.title: The table from heaven
396.hook: the disciples ask Isa for a table spread from heaven, and he prays for it (5:112–115)
396.howItsDone: Muslims know surah five as al-Ma'idah, named for this table; commentators teach the scene as Isa's prayer for provision and as a lesson that clear signs bring greater responsibility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kaffarah: the covering of a broken oath. Your line was swear less. Today, the scene that gives surah five its name.

Every surah has a name, and most are taken from a word or a scene inside it. Surah five has been called al-Ma'idah for more than a week now, the Table Spread, and so far there hasn't been a table. It arrives near the very end. Isa, Jesus son of Mary, is with his closest followers, the ones the Qur'an calls al-hawariyyun, the disciples. They've seen him heal and heard him teach. And they ask him for something that sounds, at first, almost like a dare.
screen: `AL-MA'IDAH — THE TABLE SPREAD.` → `ISA AND THE DISCIPLES.` → `A REQUEST LIKE A DARE.`

segments.voice: Verse one-twelve. The disciples say: O Isa, son of Maryam, is your Lord able to send down for us, in Pickthall's words, “a table spread with food from heaven?” Isa's first answer is a warning: be mindful of Allah, if you truly believe. So they explain, and their reasons are very human. We want to eat from it. We want our hearts at rest. We want to know for sure that you've told us the truth, and to be witnesses to it. Then Isa prays. He asks Allah to send down a table that will be a feast for them, for the first of them and the last of them, and a sign, and he ends by calling Allah the best of providers. The Arabic word for that feast is 'id, the word in Eid, and this verse is the only place it appears in the Qur'an. Allah answers: I will send it down. But whoever disbelieves after that will face a punishment like no other. A sign that clear raises the stakes for everyone who sees it. Did the table actually come down? The Qur'an gives the promise, but never narrates the table arriving, and never tells us what was on it. Early commentators disagreed. Many said yes, and passed on reports about bread and fish. Others, including the early scholars Mujahid and al-Hasan al-Basri, said that when the disciples heard the warning, they withdrew the request, and no table came. What the text does keep is the shape of a good table: a need named honestly, a prayer made for the first and the last, and the One who provides.
screen: `IS YOUR LORD ABLE?` · `HEARTS AT REST, AND WITNESSES.` · `'ID — A FEAST, FIRST AND LAST.` · `DID IT COME DOWN? THEY DIFFERED.` · then, large: `A TABLE SPREAD FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Picture a table you've eaten at that felt like more than food: a holiday, a hospital cafeteria with someone you love, a late-night kitchen. Who was there, and who set it? Then picture a small table you could set for someone else: a plate of fruit, a meal at a door, a chair pulled out for someone who usually eats alone.
Ma'idah, a table spread with food. The table the disciples asked for and Isa prayed for, a feast for the first and the last. Today's word.

397.title: Isa's answer
397.hook: on the Day, Isa answers that he only said what he was told: worship Allah, my Lord and yours (5:116–118)
397.howItsDone: Muslims read 5:116–118 as Isa's testimony on the Day of Judgment, and some recite 5:118 in night prayer, following reports that the Prophet repeated it until dawn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ma'idah: the table from heaven, the feast Isa prayed for. Your line was a table sent down. Today, Isa again, in the last scene of surah five.

A rumor grows in the retelling. A text gets screenshotted without the message before it. Someone is quoted saying what they never said, and wants one thing: to stand up and say, that's not what I said. Here's what I said, word for word. Surah five ends with a scene set not in the past but on the Day of Judgment. Allah addresses Isa, son of Maryam, directly, in front of everyone, and asks him what he told people. And Isa gives his answer, on the record.
screen: `THAT'S NOT WHAT I SAID.` → `THE DAY OF JUDGMENT.` → `ISA, ON THE RECORD.`

segments.voice: Verse one-sixteen. Allah asks: O Isa, son of Maryam, did you tell people to take you and your mother as two gods besides Allah? Isa's answer comes in layers. First, glory to You. Then: it was not for me to say what I had no right to say. If I had said it, You would know it. You know what is in my self, and I don't know what is in Yours. Then verse one-seventeen, in Pickthall's words: “I spake unto them only that which Thou commandedst me, (saying): Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.” And: I was a witness over them while I lived among them, and after You took me, You were the watcher over them. Then the last line, one-eighteen, which stands out for what it doesn't do. Isa doesn't ask for anyone to be punished. He says: if You punish them, they are Your servants, and if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise. He leaves the outcome with God. A report in the Sunan collections says the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ once spent a whole night in prayer repeating that single verse until dawn. Sahih Muslim records him reciting it and weeping for his own community. Christians describe God as one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, and do not count Mary as part of God; Muslim commentators have discussed whom the question in this verse addresses. The Qur'an's focus here is Isa himself: a prophet who said only what he was given, and then handed the rest back.

segments.voice: Think of something you've been passing along lately: a story about a coworker, a claim about the news. Ask gently: do I actually know this, or did I only hear about it? If you're not sure, picture yourself saying, I don't know, or, that's all I was told, and let that feel light, not weak.

398.title: Darkness and light
398.hook: praise to Allah who created the heavens and earth and made darkness and light (6:1)
398.howItsDone: Muslims read the opening of al-An'am as a call to see Allah in the order of creation; its first verse opens with al-hamdu lillah, as al-Fatiha does, and some recite the surah in full as a devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Isa's answer, and the end of surah five. Your line was only what I was told. Today, a new surah opens.
screen: `ISA'S ANSWER — ONLY WHAT I WAS TOLD.`

segments.voice: Surah six is al-An'am, the Cattle, named for a passage near its middle about the herds and the customs people built around them. It's a Meccan surah, from the years before the move to Medina, and tradition says it came down all at once rather than in pieces. It also opens with words you learned on day eleven of this path, the same words that open al-Fatiha: al-hamdu lillah. Then, in the very first verse, it does something quietly strange with grammar.
screen: `AL-AN'AM — THE CATTLE.` → `MECCAN, AND ALL AT ONCE.` → `IT OPENS WITH ALHAMDULILLAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in Pickthall's words: “Praise be to Allah, Who hath created the heavens and the earth, and hath appointed darkness and light.” Listen to the two verbs. The heavens and the earth are created, khalaqa. Darkness and light are appointed, made, set in place, ja'ala. Some commentators read ja'ala here as giving something its role, its job. Now the two nouns. In Arabic, darkness is plural, az-zulumat, darknesses. Light is singular, an-nur. The Qur'an keeps that shape when it uses the pair: in 2:257, Allah brings believers out of the darknesses into the light. Some commentators read it as a picture: many ways to be lost, and one way home. Later in this same surah, a verse says this is My straight path, so follow it, and don't follow the other paths that scatter you. Darknesses, many. Light, one. But the verse doesn't treat darkness as an enemy that slipped in. It opens with praise for the One who made both. Night is part of the design: the time for rest, the backdrop for stars, the dark before the dawn prayer. And the end of the verse turns, almost sadly: yet those who disbelieve set up equals to their Lord. The whole surah will keep returning to this: look at the sky, the seeds, the night and the day, and ask who set them in place. Light and darkness come first, perhaps because everyone sees them, every day, at dusk and at dawn.
screen: `CREATED, THEN APPOINTED.` · `DARKNESSES, PLURAL.` · `LIGHT, SINGULAR.` · `NIGHT IS PART OF THE DESIGN.` · then, large: `HE MADE BOTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, sit by a window at dusk, when the day is still in the sky and the dark is already coming; if not, turn off one light and leave another on. Notice the light on one side of your face and the shadow on the other, neither a mistake, each doing its job.
Az-zulumat. Darkness, in the plural: the Qur'an's word for how many ways there are to be lost, before the one path of light.
Your line: he made both. Darknesses, many; light, one; both set in place. See you tomorrow.

399.title: Not a leaf falls
399.hook: with Him are the keys of the unseen, and not a leaf falls without His knowing (6:59)
399.tomorrow: The stars, the moon, the sun, again
399.howItsDone: Belief in the ghayb, the unseen, is part of Muslim faith (2:3); scholars teach that its keys belong to Allah alone, which is why fortune-telling and horoscopes are widely discouraged.

segments.voice: Yesterday: az-zulumat wan-nur, darkness and light. Your line was he made both. A week ends today: one life, racing in good, kaffarah, the table, Isa's answer, darkness and light. Now one small leaf.

A big tree lets go of more leaves in one autumn than anyone could count. Nobody tries; the groundskeeper with the leaf blower certainly doesn't. Each one lets go at its own moment, twists on the way down, lands, and is gone under the next. Of all the pictures the Qur'an could have picked to say Allah knows everything, verse fifty-nine of surah six reaches for that one. Not a mountain. Not a galaxy. A leaf.
screen: `MORE LEAVES THAN ANYONE COUNTS.` → `NOBODY COUNTS THEM.` → `THE QUR'AN PICKS A LEAF.`

segments.voice: The verse begins: with Him are the keys of the unseen, and no one knows them but He. The word for the unseen is ghayb: what is absent, hidden, out of sight; words from the same family describe someone who's away. Belief in the ghayb is one of the first things the Qur'an says about the mindful, at the start of surah two: they believe in the unseen. Then the verse moves from the cosmic to the small. He knows what is in the land and the sea. In Pickthall's words: “Not a leaf falleth but He knoweth it,” not a grain in the darkness of the earth, nothing wet or dry, but it's in a clear record. A hadith in Bukhari says the keys of the unseen are five, and the Prophet ﷺ then recited the last verse of surah thirty-one: the knowledge of the Hour, the sending of rain, what is in the womb, what a person will earn tomorrow, and in what land a person will die. Things people long to know, and can't. Muslim scholars cite this hadith to draw a line: no fortune-teller and no horoscope holds those keys. So the verse does two things at once. It humbles: you don't hold the keys. And, in the verse's telling, it comforts: nothing goes unnoticed. Not the job you didn't get, not the hour you spent awake, not the small kindness no one saw. Not a single leaf.
screen: `GHAYB — THE HIDDEN, THE ABSENT.` · `THE KEYS OF THE UNSEEN.` · `THE FIVE THAT NO ONE KNOWS.` · `HUMBLING, AND COMFORTING.` · then, large: `NOT A LEAF FALLETH BUT HE KNOWETH IT.`

segments.voice: If you can see a tree or a plant, watch one leaf; if not, picture one, and follow it with your eyes as long as you can. Then let your attention widen to all the other leaves, on all the other trees, in every city, right now, each one moving, with nobody you know watching them. Breathe with that.
Ghayb. The unseen: what is hidden from us, whose keys are with Allah alone, and not a leaf falls without His knowing. Today's word.
Your line: not a leaf unknown. The small, unseen moments count too. I'm glad you came.
